cues.text: A Church with Three Popes
Since 1378, the Catholic Church had been torn by the Western Schism , with rival popes elected by competing factions of cardinals and recognized by different kingdoms of Europe.
A council held at Pisa in 1409 had attempted to resolve the crisis by deposing both existing claimants and electing a third.

Neither deposed pope accepted the verdict, leaving Christendom with three simultaneous claimants to the Chair of Peter: Gregory XII in Rome, Benedict XIII in Avignon and Spain, and John XXIII , the Pisan line's second pope.
Under pressure from the Holy Roman Emperor-elect Sigismund , John XXIII reluctantly summoned a new general council to meet at Constance .
He hoped to secure his own position; instead, the council he convened would ultimately depose him along with his rivals.
Ending the Schism
The council opened on November 5, 1414 and grew into the largest assembly medieval Christendom had ever seen.
Several hundred bishops, dozens of cardinals, hundreds of doctors of theology and law, and numerous secular princes attended.
They voted for the first time by nation rather than by head, preventing any single kingdom's bishops from dominating proceedings.
Sensing the council's hostility, John XXIII fled Constance in disguise in March 1415, but was captured, brought back, and formally deposed.

Gregory XII, recognizing the council's legitimacy on the condition that he himself first formally reconvene it, then abdicated voluntarily in July 1415 — the only one of the three claimants to resign willingly.
Benedict XIII refused to yield and was declared deposed in absentia in 1417.
With the field finally clear, the council elected Cardinal Oddone Colonna as Pope Martin V in November 1417, ending nearly forty years of division.
The Condemnation of Jan Hus
Alongside the schism, the council addressed the teachings of the English reformer John Wyclif , already dead but posthumously condemned.
It also addressed the Bohemian reformer Jan Hus , who had drawn on Wyclif's ideas to criticize clerical wealth, indulgences, and aspects of Eucharistic theology.
Hus traveled to Constance under a promise of safe conduct from Emperor Sigismund, hoping to defend his views before the assembled fathers.
The council instead tried him for heresy and condemned his teachings.
Despite the safe conduct, which the council held did not extend to a convicted heretic, it handed him over to secular authorities.
They burned him at the stake on July 6, 1415 .
His execution, widely seen in Bohemia as a betrayal of the emperor's word, ignited the Hussite Wars that convulsed Central Europe for the following two decades.
Conciliarism and Reform
In its early sessions, before Martin V's election, the council issued the decrees Haec Sancta and Frequens .
Haec Sancta asserted that a general council holds authority directly from Christ and that even a pope must obey it in matters of faith.
Frequens mandated that general councils be held at regular intervals thereafter.
These decrees expressed a theory known as conciliarism , which held that supreme authority in the Church rests with an ecumenical council rather than with the pope alone.
Martin V, once elected, accepted the council's practical achievements but never fully endorsed the broader conciliarist theory.
Subsequent popes worked steadily to reassert papal primacy over the following decades, a tension that would not be fully resolved until much later councils.
Legacy

Constance's achievement in ending the Western Schism ranks among the most significant institutional accomplishments of any medieval council, restoring a single, universally recognized papacy after forty years of division that had scandalized and confused ordinary believers across Europe.
Its treatment of Hus, however, remains one of the most painful episodes in the era of the councils.
Six centuries later, in 1999, Pope St. John Paul II expressed "deep regret" for Hus's death, a rare papal acknowledgment of the tragic consequences of the council's harshest judgment.
